evidence.observation: The added table-driven contract block for the coding-agent settings resolver. It declares a `fixtures` array (lines 673-736) where each row supplies `user` (agentDir/settings.json), `project` (projectDir/.pi/settings.json), and `cli` (applyOverrides) partial settings plus expected resolved values, and a single `it.each(fixtures)` assertion (lines 738-753) that runs every row. For each fixture it writes the user and project files, calls SettingsManager.create(projectDir, agentDir), and asserts the project value wins over the user/default value; it then calls manager.applyOverrides(cli) and asserts the explicit CLI value wins over the project value. Fixtures cover defaultModel, theme, shellCommandPrefix, defaultTools, httpIdleTimeoutMs, and outputPad.

The executable assertion at the heart of the contract. The body (lines 741-742) writes the user/global settings and the project settings to disk, line 744 constructs the resolver via SettingsManager.create, line 747 asserts `read(manager)` equals the project value (project beats user/default), line 750 applies the explicit CLI value via manager.applyOverrides(cli), and line 751 asserts `read(manager)` now equals the CLI value (CLI beats project). This is the direct, observable precedence contract.

Pre-existing precedent for the same resolver contract: the 'loads global defaults and lets project settings replace them' case writes a global defaultTools list, asserts it is read back, then writes a project defaultTools list and asserts the project value replaces the global one. It establishes the project-beats-user/default half of the contract that the new table-driven block extends with the explicit-CLI-beats-project half.

The resolver entry point exercised by the test. It resolves cwd/agentDir, builds a FileSettingsStorage, and loads global settings from `agentDir/settings.json` (line 363) and project settings from `cwd/.pi/settings.json` (line 364), so the test files written at those exact paths are the two lower-precedence sources.

The explicit-CLI override channel: `applyOverrides(overrides)` replaces this.settings with deepMergeSettings(this.settings, overrides), merging the CLI values on top of the already-merged global+project settings. Because it is applied last and mutates the same `settings` field the getters read, CLI values win over project values. It does not touch globalSettings/projectSettings, so the override is an in-memory, non-persisted value - exactly the CLI-flag semantics the assertion checks.

The precedence rule itself: 'project/overrides take precedence, nested objects merge recursively'. It delegates to deepMergeObjects, so a scalar or array project/CLI value replaces the lower-precedence value while nested objects merge - which is why each fixture's scalar/array setting resolves to the higher-precedence source.

Representative public getter used by the fixtures: it reads this.settings.defaultTools - the single merged/resolved object - and returns a copy. Because every fixture getter (getDefaultModel, getTheme, getShellCommandPrefix, getHttpIdleTimeoutMs, getOutputPad, getDefaultTools) reads this.settings, both precedence transitions (project over user, CLI over project) are observable through the public API rather than internal state.

claims.claim: The added `describe("setting precedence")` block is a table-driven assertion: one `it.each(fixtures)` case runs a fixture table that supplies user/default, project, and explicit CLI values and reads the resolved value back through public getters.

For every fixture the project value wins over the user/default value, and an explicit CLI value applied via applyOverrides wins over the project value - i.e. precedence is CLI > project > user/default.

The two precedence steps are grounded in the resolver: SettingsManager.create deep-merges project settings over global/user settings, and applyOverrides deep-merges CLI values last on top of the merged settings, both via deepMergeSettings/deepMergeObjects.
